analysis.one_liner: Creates a new federal commission to regulate digital platforms, covering competition, consumer protection, and child safety.
analysis.headline: The bill to create a federal regulator for big digital platforms never got a vote; it died in the Senate Commerce Committee with only two sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Digital Platform Commission Act would create a new federal agency, the Federal Digital Platform Commission, to regulate online platforms like social media networks, search engines, and marketplaces. The commission could write rules on competition, algorithmic transparency, age-appropriate design for children, and data practices, designate the largest platforms as "systemically important," and weigh in on their mergers. It would also let individuals and state attorneys general sue platforms and impose penalties of up to 15% of a platform's global annual revenue. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users would gain a regulator with power over the largest platforms: rules requiring age-appropriate design and age verification to protect children, transparency and auditing of recommendation algorithms, data portability and interoperability standards that make it easier to leave a dominant platform, and accessibility standards for people with disabilities. Small businesses that depend on dominant platforms to reach customers would benefit from merger scrutiny and from rules aimed at preventing exclusion from platforms. Local journalism, which the bill's findings say has been undercut by dominant platforms, and independent researchers, who would get access to platform data through a research office and grant program, would also benefit. Small digital platform businesses and news organizations are explicitly excluded from regulation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Online users, kids, and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a Federal Digital Platform Commission with rulemaking, investigative, and enforcement authority over digital platforms, closing a regulatory gap that has existed since the Telecommunications Act of 1996.

Requires the commission to write an age-appropriate design code and age verification standards within 180 days of the first commissioners being confirmed, aimed at protecting minors from addictive design and data harvesting.

Directs the commission to set data portability and interoperability standards and to require fairness, transparency, auditing, and explainability for the recommendation algorithms of the largest platforms — making it easier for users to switch services and harder for platforms to run opaque, biased systems.

Creates a 'systemically important digital platform' designation, with criteria including the platform's power over news dissemination, market power, daily users, and small businesses' dependence on it, triggering the strictest rules and mandatory pre-merger notifications with recommendations the FTC and Justice Department must give substantial weight to.

Lets any person damaged by a platform file a complaint with the commission or sue in federal court, lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents, and allows the commission to order restitution and civil penalties capped at 15% of a platform's global annual revenue — with daily forfeitures of up to 1% of global revenue for missed reporting deadlines.
Imposes conflict-of-interest rules on commissioners and staff, bars them from owning securities of regulated companies, and bars commissioners from other employment while serving.

Establishes a Code Council split evenly among platform representatives, public-interest representatives and academics, and technical experts, to propose rules in a public process with comment periods; small digital platform businesses and news organizations are excluded from the definition of regulated platforms.

analysis.who_pays: Large digital platforms — social media networks, search engines, e-commerce marketplaces — would bear the direct costs: compliance with new design, transparency, interoperability, and auditing rules, mandatory merger reviews, and penalties of up to 15% of global annual revenue per year. Taxpayers would fund the new agency, with appropriations rising from $100 million in fiscal 2023 to $500 million per year by fiscal 2027. Ordinary users would face some friction from age verification requirements, and platforms would likely pass compliance costs to the businesses that sell through them. Small platforms and news organizations are carved out.

drawbacks.text: The new agency would cost taxpayers between $100 million and $500 million per year in authorized appropriations, rising to $500 million annually for fiscal years 2027 through 2032.

Jurisdiction is broad: the bill covers nearly any online service that facilitates interactions between users and sellers, with the commission deciding which platforms to forbear from regulating based on size and other attributes. That discretion could either sweep in services with little public-stakes or, conversely, be exercised to spare favored incumbents.

Because platforms carry speech, any commission rules touching content moderation and algorithmic ranking would face First Amendment legal challenges; the bill itself acknowledges regulation must remain consistent with the First Amendment, and courts, not the commission, would likely have the final word for years.

The process is slow by design: a proposed code moves through a council with 180 to 360 days just to vote on a recommendation, then a 45-to-90-day public comment period before the commission acts, and an independent panel would evaluate the commission after five years and recommend whether it should continue at all.
Age verification standards would require users to prove their age online, raising its own privacy questions for ordinary people even as it protects children.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an unusually detailed attempt to give ordinary users, children, and small businesses real leverage over the handful of companies that control the online public square and marketplace, with genuine structural safeguards: carve-outs for small businesses and news organizations, conflict-of-interest bans for commissioners, a balanced industry-public-expert council, and a five-year sunset review. The honest costs are real but modest relative to the stakes: several hundred million dollars a year in taxpayer funding, years of litigation over any rule touching speech, and a slow multi-step rulemaking process that delays benefits. The bigger design question is whether a single new agency could move fast enough against companies that change their products weekly. The public never got an answer, because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet, joined by Senator Peter Welch, introduced the Digital Platform Commission Act on May 18, 2023, proposing a five-member commission to regulate digital platforms with $100 million in first-year funding rising to $500 million per year.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which was its only committee action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the bill attracted only one cosponsor and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large digital platforms came out ahead: they remain without a dedicated federal regulator, and the algorithmic transparency, interoperability, child-safety, and merger rules the bill would have imposed never took effect. Taxpayers also avoided the cost of funding a new agency.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, proposing a new Federal Digital Platform Commission with rulemaking and enforcement power over digital platforms.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor; the bill was introduced for Bennet and Welch together.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 18, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Large technology platforms and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the wave of platform-regulation and antitrust bills in the 118th Congress; this bill never reached a stage where their opposition had to be overcome.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its only two sponsors were Democrats, and it never advanced far enough to reveal whether support or opposition split by party.

industries.industry: Large digital platforms (social media, search, e-commerce)
industries.note: The bill would subject the biggest platforms to a dedicated regulator, mandatory algorithmic transparency and auditing, interoperability and data portability standards, pre-merger review, and civil penalties up to 15% of global annual revenue. These companies currently write their own rules, as the bill's findings state, and would lose that position.

The bill targets the practice of monetizing personal data without informed consent, listed among the harms in its findings, and its age-appropriate design code and privacy-focused design rules would restrict behavioral data collection that ad-tech depends on.

The bill exempts small digital platform businesses, as defined by the Small Business Administration, and excludes de minimis online offerings, sparing startups compliance costs. It would also give them interoperability rights against dominant incumbents, though enforcement would depend on the commission's forbearance choices.

News organizations are excluded from the definition of regulated platforms, and the bill's findings cite the role of dominant platforms in the collapse of trusted local journalism; rules on the platforms' power over news dissemination were aimed partly at this problem.
